outcomes.original: Filing step: If the zoning determination confirms CUA is required, file a pre-application meeting request with SF Planning and schedule community outreach. What to say: Schedule a pre-application meeting with the assigned SF Planning case planner. Present the existing restaurant use history (the 1981 ABC license and any lease or business-license records showing continuous operation), the proposed enlargement into the laundromat space, and the limited-cooking, no-alcohol concept. Ask whether the project qualifies for any fee waivers (e.g., First Year Free for new storefronts). Begin neighbor outreach: meet with the Nob Hill Neighborhood Association and owners/tenants within 300 feet before filing the formal CUA application, and document their feedback to address concerns in the application narrative.
outcomes.note: The record is a CUA at a different address and does not state the ABC license, laundromat space, fee waivers, neighborhood association, or 300-foot outreach requirement.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with SF Planning, including the laundromat-removal justification and non-conforming use analysis. What to say: Submit the CUA application online via SF Planning's portal, including: (1) Project narrative explaining that the restaurant use has existed at 1148 & 1152 Taylor since at least 1981 (cite the ABC license), has not been abandoned, and the enlargement into the adjacent laundromat space serves neighborhood demand without displacing housing. Address Planning Code §202.12 laundromat removal by noting the laundromat portion is no longer operating and the restaurant expansion maintains ground-floor commercial activity. (2) Site plans, floor plans and elevations showing the existing 1,718 sq ft restaurant area and the proposed 2,290 sq ft combined space with limited kitchen, seating layout and any new signage. outcomes.original: Filing step: Complete the Planning Department's environmental review and any neighborhood notification required by Planning Code §311 or §312. What to say: Work with the Planning case planner to complete the environmental evaluation (typically a categorical exemption for interior tenant improvements and minor use changes). If §311 neighborhood notification applies (likely for a CU in RM-3), mail notice to all property owners and occupants within 300 feet at least 30 days before the hearing, post a yellow notice at the site, and publish the notice as directed by Planning. Respond to any Discretionary Review requests or neighbor comments by the deadline set in the notification process.
outcomes.note: The record shows a CU case in RM-3 zoning but does not state any of the notification requirements, distances, timing, or procedures described.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Attend the Planning Commission hearing and present the project, emphasizing compatibility with the residential neighborhood and continuation of existing use. What to say: At the Planning Commission hearing (held on Thursday afternoons), present a 5-minute summary: 'Nob Hill Cafe has operated at this location since at least 1981 with a beer-and-wine license. The proposed enlargement into the adjacent closed laundromat maintains ground-floor neighborhood-serving retail, avoids displacement of housing, and operates with limited cooking and no late-night hours. The low density of restaurants in the area (only 2 food/drink businesses within 500 feet) and the enclosed interior improvements minimize any impact on neighboring residents. We have met with nearby owners and commit to hours of operation ending by 10 p.m., no amplified music, and a community liaison during construction.' If commissioners raise concerns about non-conforming use expansion, offer to accept conditions limiting further expansion and codifying the hours and no-alcohol operation.
outcomes.note: The cited records are CUA approvals at other addresses but do not contain the facts stated about hearing schedules, presentation times, the cafe's history, the laundromat, or business density.

outcomes.original: Filing step: If the CUA is approved, wait through the 30-day appeal period, then obtain the signed Motion and Conditions of Approval from Planning. What to say: After the Planning Commission approves the CUA, the decision is subject to a 30-day appeal period to the Board of Supervisors. Monitor the appeal window (Planning will notify you of any appeal filed). If no appeal is filed, request the signed Motion and Conditions of Approval from Planning, which will list all operating restrictions (hours, expansion limits, community liaison, etc.). You will need this document to apply for the building permit, health permit and any future ABC license.
outcomes.note: The record shows only an approved CUA case at a different address with no procedural information about appeals, documents, or subsequent permit requirements.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the building permit application with SF DBI, routing it to Planning for zoning sign-off and to DPH for plan check. What to say: Submit the building permit application online via SF DBI's portal, including: (1) Architectural plans stamped by a California-licensed architect showing the tenant improvements (kitchen equipment, finishes, restrooms, exits, ADA compliance). (2) The CUA Motion and Conditions of Approval. (3) DPH plan-check submittal (two sets of scaled drawings, equipment spec sheets, finishes schedule, and menu) routed to the Environmental Health Branch. Request routing to Planning (§175 referral), DPH, SFFD (for hood suppression system), and SFPUC (for grease interceptor review). Pay the building permit fee (percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–$3,000 for a restaurant TI) and the DPH plan-check fee ($828–$2,207 depending on scope). Allow 21–60 days for DPH plan review and 14–120 days for building permit approval.
outcomes.note: Records give time ranges (21–60 days DPH, 14–120 days building permit) and DPH fee ($828–$2,207), but not the specific filing procedures, routing instructions, or the narrowed building permit fee range of $800–$3,000.

outcomes.original: Filing step: After DPH plan approval and building permit issuance, complete construction and schedule the DPH pre-final and final inspections. What to say: During construction, coordinate with your architect and licensed subcontractors (plumber, electrician, mechanical) to obtain their permits and inspections. Install the grease interceptor per SFPUC specifications and submit the Installation Verification Form to earn the sewer-bill discount. At approximately 80% construction completion, email your DPH plan reviewer to schedule a pre-final inspection (at least two weeks' notice). Address any corrections, then schedule the final DPH inspection (two weeks' notice) and the DBI final inspection. Ensure a certified food safety manager is on staff and all employees have California Food Handler Cards before the DPH final. Apply for the Health Permit to Operate ($470 application fee, $0 annual license fee for 2026–28) and the SF Business Registration Certificate ($55–$95 depending on gross receipts) before opening.
outcomes.note: Records support grease interceptor installation, Installation Verification Form, certified manager requirement, and health permit fees ($470 application, $0 annual for 2026-28), but not the specific timings, notice periods, employee food handler cards, or business registration details.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,150 to $17,500. Notes: Timeline is 120–300 days from CUA filing to approval, representing the time to obtain a Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days per catalog entry sf.conditional_use_authorization inferred from comparable case 2015-006347CUA, which took 189 days) and the health permit (14–45 days per catalog sf.health_permit), when they are granted. Cost range covers the CUA application fee (approximately $3,150 in 2023 for a project with tenant improvements, CPI-adjusted from the 2023–24 schedule), the building permit with TI ($800–$15,000 per catalog sf.building_permit), DPH plan check ($828–$2,500 per catalog sf.health_plan_check), health permit to operate ($470–$1,000 per catalog sf.health_permit), FOG registration ($0–$500 per catalog sf.fog_wastewater_permit), sign permit ($300–$1,500 per catalog sf.sign_permit), and SF business registration ($55–$700 per catalog sf.business_registration). This timeline and cost apply only if the CUA is approved; they do not cover denial or withdrawal. The timeline does not include pre-application preparation, neighbor outreach or the 30-day appeal period after Commission approval, so plan for an additional 60–90 days before and after the hearing. If the zoning determination in step 1 concludes no CUA is required (for example, if the property qualifies under §231 Limited Corner Commercial Use and the expansion is allowed), the timeline drops to 14–120 days for the building permit and health permit alone, with costs of $800–$15,000 for the building permit, $828–$2,500 for DPH plan check, $470–$1,000 for the health permit, and the other minor fees listed above.
